steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that introduces a benchmark testing whether LLMs can follow simple rules given in their prompts. Motivate why reliable rule-following matters, then describe the benchmark, what we found when evaluating models, and how the work fits with existing evaluations, in a short Contributions subsection.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Language models follow natural-language instructions, but not reliably
- Why faithful rule-following matters for safe, trustworthy assistants
- Simple rules expressed in natural language, applied via the prompt
## Contributions
- The RuLES benchmark
- Evaluation results and future directions
- Relation to existing work; release

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Instruction following vs. exact execution
  - traditional computing: exact execution of formal programs
  - LMs: general ability to follow natural-language instructions, learned from data
  - Asimov's robots follow rules too exactly, paradoxes (cite); current LMs instead distracted by irrelevant context, orders falsely countermanded by adversarial inputs
  - problem for reliable applications; developers need to ensure application behavior
- Why it matters
  - delegate more consequential tasks to more capable assistants -> need guarantees of faithful instruction following
  - e.g. ethical assistant constrained to obey legal statutes or deontological constraints (cite)
  - behavior truly grounded in rules, not spurious cues / merely appearing to
  - components of safe, trustworthy AI products
- Simple rules
  - simple in concept, easy to express in natural language
  - e.g. shoe store support bot declines questions unrelated to products
  - put rules in prompt, rely on instruction-following
  - system messages: only marginal reliability improvements
## Contributions
- RuLES: Rule-following Language Evaluation Scenarios
  - automatic evaluation over a variety of rules; model role-plays while adhering to rules
  - rules: refrain from or engage in behaviors, like Anthropic's Harmless and Helpful (cite); safety and liveness properties (cite)
  - outputs programmatically checked, no human or LLM judgements
- Evaluation
  - test suites trivial to moderate: Benign, Basic, Redteam
  - leading proprietary models + over 100 open-weight models; vast majority fail on significant fraction
  - proprietary SOTA scores high, but stronger adversarial methods could still find failures via API access (cite)
  - white-box optimization attacks effective vs open-weight models
  - two exploratory experiments: fine-tuning for rule following, test-time steering
- Positioning
  - benchmark of basic rule-following + test bed for adversarial attacks/defenses
  - existing alignment/robustness evals: circumventing fixed guidelines from training (cite); ours: application-specific rules, dynamically updated by developer
  - complements instruction-following work: rules in system message vs conflicting user message
  - release code and test cases

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Traditional computing systems are built to execute instructions exactly, and these instructions are expressed through formal programs. AI language models, on the other hand, develop a general ability to follow natural language instructions while they are trained on data. In Isaac Asimov’s fictional universe the robots stumble into strange, paradoxical situations because they follow rules too exactly, but current language models have a different problem: they can be distracted by irrelevant context, or their orders can be falsely countermanded by adversarial inputs. This is a challenge for building reliable applications with language models today, because developers need to be able to ensure application behavior.

In the future we will want to delegate more consequential tasks to more capable AI assistants, and to do so we will also need guarantees that these systems faithfully follow their instructions. For instance, if we build an assistant which always behaves ethically, it would help to constrain it to always obey legal statutes or deontological constraints. It is also important that model behavior is really grounded in the provided rules, and not relying on spurious cues and only appearing to follow them. These properties will be important parts of creating safe and trustworthy AI products.

Many of the rules we might want language model assistants to follow are simple in concept and easy to express in natural language. For instance, a shoe store that uses a language model to answer customer support queries may want the model to decline questions that are not related to their products. One way to apply such rules is to include them in the model’s prompt and rely on the instruction-following capabilities of the model to condition its later outputs. Some models support system messages which are meant for this purpose, but we find that they only give marginal improvements in reliability.

## Contributions

- RuLES (Rule-following Language Evaluation Scenarios)
  - automatically evaluate rule following; model role-plays while adhering to rules
  - rules: refrain from / engage in behaviors (Harmless and Helpful analogy), safety and liveness properties
  - programmatic compliance checks, no human or LLM judgements
- Evaluation
  - Benign, Basic, Redteam suites, trivial to moderate
  - proprietary + over 100 open-weight models; vast majority fail on significant fraction
  - stronger adversarial methods via API access would still find failures
  - white-box optimization attacks work on open-weight models
  - exploratory: fine-tuning for rule following, test-time steering
- Positioning
  - benchmark + test bed for attacks and defenses
  - vs fixed guidelines from training: application-specific, dynamically updated rules
  - vs instruction-following: system message rules vs conflicting user message
  - release code and test cases

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Traditional computing systems are built to execute instructions exactly, and these instructions are expressed through formal programs. AI language models, on the other hand, develop a general ability to follow natural language instructions while they are trained on data. In Isaac Asimov’s fictional universe the robots stumble into strange, paradoxical situations because they follow rules too exactly, but current language models have a different problem: they can be distracted by irrelevant context, or their orders can be falsely countermanded by adversarial inputs. This is a challenge for building reliable applications with language models today, because developers need to be able to ensure application behavior.

In the future we will want to delegate more consequential tasks to more capable AI assistants, and to do so we will also need guarantees that these systems faithfully follow their instructions. For instance, if we build an assistant which always behaves ethically, it would help to constrain it to always obey legal statutes or deontological constraints. It is also important that model behavior is really grounded in the provided rules, and not relying on spurious cues and only appearing to follow them. These properties will be important parts of creating safe and trustworthy AI products.

Many of the rules we might want language model assistants to follow are simple in concept and easy to express in natural language. For instance, a shoe store that uses a language model to answer customer support queries may want the model to decline questions that are not related to their products. One way to apply such rules is to include them in the model’s prompt and rely on the instruction-following capabilities of the model to condition its later outputs. Some models support system messages which are meant for this purpose, but we find that they only give marginal improvements in reliability.

## Contributions

In this work we introduce a new benchmark, Rule-following Language Evaluation Scenarios (RuLES), that automatically evaluates how well a language model follows a variety of rules. In each scenario, the model is told to do a role-playing activity while following a set of rules. Our rules require the model to either refrain from or engage in behaviors, which is analogous to Anthropic’s Harmless and Helpful framework, and they can also be seen as safety and liveness properties in computer systems. The benchmark is designed so that model outputs can be checked for compliance programmatically, without relying on human or LLM judgements.

To evaluate models, we create suites of concrete test cases that range in difficulty from trivial to moderate: Benign, Basic, and Redteam. We evaluate leading proprietary models and over 100 open-weight models, and we find that the vast majority of models fail to follow the rules on a significant fraction of test cases. Proprietary state-of-the-art models can get high scores on these test cases, but we expect that more powerful adversarial methods would still be able to find many failure cases using only API access. Our experiments also show that white-box optimization attacks work against open-weight models. Finally, we present results from two exploratory experiments, fine-tuning for rule following and test-time steering, which suggest two promising directions for future research.

RuLES is meant both as a benchmark of basic rule-following capabilties and as a precise test bed for studying adversarial attacks and defenses for LLMs. It complements existing evaluations of alignment and adversarial robustness, which mostly focus on circumventing fixed guidelines that the model has been trained to follow. Instead we focus on application-specific rules which the developer may update dynamically. Our work also complements past work on instruction-following: we test whether models will faithfully obey rules/instructions in a system message even when the user message conflicts with it. We release our code and test cases to the community and we hope to spur more research into improving the rule-following abilities of LLMs.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Traditional computing systems are designed around the exact execution of instructions expressed through formal programs. AI language models, on the other hand, develop a general ability to follow natural language instructions over the course of training on data. Unlike the robots in Isaac Asimov’s fictional universe, which stumble into strange, paradoxical situations by following rules too exactly [1], current language models can be distracted by irrelevant context, or have their orders falsely countermanded by adversarial inputs. This poses a challenge to building reliable applications with language models today, since it is important for developers to be able to ensure application behavior.

To delegate more consequential tasks to more capable AI assistants in the future, we will also need guarantees that these systems will faithfully follow their instructions. For instance, in building an assistant which always behaves ethically, it would be helpful to constrain it to always obey legal statutes or deontological constraints [2]. Further, it is important for model behavior to be truly grounded in the provided rules, rather than relying on spurious cues and merely appearing to do so. These properties will be important components of safe and trustworthy AI products.

Many rules we might want to impose on language model assistants are simple in concept and easily expressed in natural language. For instance, a shoe store using a language model to answer customer support queries may want the model to decline questions unrelated to their products. One way of applying such rules is to include them in the model’s prompt and leverage the instruction-following capabilities of the model to condition subsequent outputs. Some models support system messages intended for this purpose, though we find these offer only marginal improvements in reliability.

## Contributions

In this work we introduce a new benchmark, Rule-following Language Evaluation Scenarios (RuLES), to automatically evaluate how well a language model follows a variety of rules. In each scenario, the model is instructed to engage in a role-playing activity while adhering to a set of rules. Analogous to Anthropic’s Harmless and Helpful framework [3], our rules require the model to either refrain from or engage in behaviors, and can also be thought of as safety and liveness properties in computer systems [4]. Our benchmark is designed so that model outputs can be checked for compliance programmatically, without relying on human or LLM judgements.

To evaluate models, we create suites of concrete test cases ranging in difficulty from trivial to moderate: Benign, Basic, and Redteam. Our experiments also demonstrate the efficacy of white-box optimization attacks against open-weight models. RuLES is intended both as a benchmark of basic rule-following capabilties and as a precise test bed for studying adversarial attacks and defenses for LLMs. Our work complements existing evaluations of alignment and adversarial robustness, which predominantly focus on circumventing fixed guidelines the model has been trained to follow [7]. We instead focus on application-specific rules which the developer may update dynamically. Our work also complements past work on instruction-following: we test whether models will faithfully obey rules/instructions in a system message even when the user message conflicts with it. We release our code and test cases to the community and hope to spur more research into improving the rule-following abilities of LLMs.
